title: Git Undo Explained: reset vs revert vs restore (with reflog recovery)

sentences: You just ran git commit, and the second it finished, you realised it was wrong.
Maybe it's the wrong file. Maybe it's the wrong branch. Maybe it's already pushed.
Git has four tools for this: restore, reset, revert, and reflog.
They look similar, but they do very different things. Pick the wrong one, and you can lose work, or rewrite history your team depends on.
Every Git mistake becomes easier once you ask one question: which place changed?
There are three. The working directory, where your files are. The index, also called the staging area. And the repository, where commits are stored.
HEAD points to the commit you are currently on.
Each undo command touches a different combination of these places.
Keep that picture in mind, because every command that follows moves something between these three places.
Start with the smallest tool: git restore.
If you edited a file and want it back the way it was, git restore, then the file name, discards that change from the working directory.
If you already ran git add, git restore with the staged flag moves the file back out of the index, but keeps your edit.
Restore never touches your commits. It only fixes the files and the index.
Now say you made a commit and want to undo it. That's git reset.
Reset moves your branch back to an earlier commit. What happens to your changes depends on the mode.
With soft, the branch moves, but your changes stay staged, ready to commit again.
With mixed, the default, the branch moves and the index resets, so your changes stay in your files, but unstaged.
With hard, everything resets: the branch, the index, and your files. Your changes are gone from the working directory.
One more detail: hard reset does not delete untracked files.
Reset is fine for commits that only exist on your machine.
But if the bad commit is already pushed to a shared branch, do not rewrite history.
Use git revert. It creates a brand new commit that applies the opposite change.
The original bad commit stays in history, so everyone's copy still lines up, and nobody has to repair their branch.
Now the scary one. You ran reset hard, and your commit disappeared from the log.
It isn't gone. Git keeps a local journal of where HEAD has been, called the reflog.
Run git reflog, find the line for your lost commit, and reset hard back to it.
The reflog is local, and old entries expire eventually, so recover quickly.
Let's replay it in a throwaway repository. Three commits: A, B, and C, where C is the mistake.
First, git reset soft, HEAD tilde one. The log now ends at B, and git status shows the change staged, with the letter M in the first column.
Start over, and run git reset mixed instead. Same commit history, but now the M sits in the second column. The change is in the file, unstaged.
Start over, and run git reset hard. Git status is empty, and the file is back to how it looked at B.
Now the rescue. Git reflog shows the reset, and right below it, the commit called C, oops.
Reset hard to HEAD at one, in braces, and the file is back. That is the safety net, working.
Three mistakes show up again and again.
One: resetting a commit that is already pushed, then force-pushing. Teammates' branches now disagree with yours. If you must force-push, use force with lease, and tell the team first.
Two: running reset hard with edits you never committed. The reflog tracks commits, so changes that were never committed are generally gone for good.
Three: believing revert removes a secret. It doesn't. The old commit stays in history, so rotate the credential first, then clean history if needed.
Interviewers rarely ask for command names. They ask for scenarios.
For example: a faulty commit is on protected main, and it has already deployed.
A strong answer follows a framework: impact, evidence, investigation, immediate mitigation, communication, permanent fix, and prevention.
Here, the mitigation is git revert, because main is shared. The permanent fix is a tested change, and prevention is branch protection and required checks.
Notice the order: stabilise production first, then investigate, and only then fix the cause.
Reading is not enough. Practise in a safe sandbox.
The Git Command Master Map repository has an undo and reflog lab, where every destructive command runs in a disposable repository.
The link is in the description.
Recap: restore fixes files. Reset moves your branch. Revert undoes safely on shared branches. Reflog saves you when you slip.

Reset soft, mixed, or hard. What is the difference?
Say you committed the wrong thing, and you want to undo it.
All three modes move your branch back one commit.
Soft keeps your changes staged, ready to commit again.
Mixed keeps them in your files, but unstaged.
Hard throws them away, and resets your files to match.
Slipped? Git reflog keeps a journal of where your branch has been.
Find the lost commit there, and reset hard back to it.
